paper_title: QFabric: Guarded Cross-Domain Task Recovery and Its Limits on a Linux-RTOS Board

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Heterogeneous embedded boards pair a Linux application processor with a real-time microcontroller (MCU), which suggests moving a task between the two domains when its timing degrades. We present QFabric, a prototype that treats cross-domain placement as guarded recovery from a violated empirical soft real-time contract: a bounded task is compiled for both domains, monitored in windows with hysteresis, switched only after semantic and capacity admission at a quiescent epoch boundary, and committed or rolled back after probation. On an Arduino UNO Q (Cortex-A53 Linux and a Cortex-M33 running Zephyr), we characterize the stock Bridge RPC interconnect and measure five workloads in both domains under idle, CPU-load, and higher-priority SCHED_FIFO contention, with ordinary and real-time callers. Each MCU invocation costs about 19 ms of dispatch regardless of compute, the MCU runs the heaviest kernel 34x slower, and because every call traverses Linux userspace, Linux contention inflates the MCU path far more than the Linux path (p99 up to 400 ms versus 17.0 ms). Across 30 cells of a four-node chain, Linux meets every contract within 0.8% misses and QFabric correctly never migrates; a controller without hysteresis migrates in 7 cells, raising p95 by up to 177x, and probation rolls back 5 of those moves. On Linux-dispatched heterogeneous boards, migration therefore cannot isolate a task from Linux interference, and recovery guards matter chiefly by preventing harmful moves. This paper supersedes an earlier artifact release whose reported improvement arose from measurement defects that we identify. All source, raw traces, and generators are public.

CSE, JIS University anwesha.elixpo@gmail.com AbstractHeterogeneous embedded boards pair Linux application processor with real-time microcontroller (MCU), which suggests moving task between the two domains when its timing degrades. We present QFabric, prototype that treats cross-domain placement as guarded recovery from violated empirical soft real-time contract: bounded task is compiled for both domains, monitored in windows with hysteresis, switched only after semantic and capacity admission at quiescent epoch boundary, and committed or rolled back after probation. On an Arduino UNO (Cortex-A53 Linux and Cortex-M33 running Zephyr), we characterize the stock Bridge RPC interconnect and measure five workloads in both domains under idle, CPU-load, and higher-priority SCHED_FIFO contention, with ordinary and real-time callers. Each MCU invocation costs about 19 ms of dispatch regardless of compute, the MCU runs the heaviest kernel 34 slower, and because every call traverses Linux userspace, Linux contention inflates the MCU path far more than the Linux path (p99 up to 400 ms versus 17.0 ms). Across 30 cells of fournode chain, Linux meets every contract within 0.8% misses and QFabric correctly never migrates; controller without hysteresis migrates in 7 cells, raising p95 by up to 177, and probation rolls back 5 of those moves. On Linux-dispatched heterogeneous boards, migration therefore cannot isolate task from Linux interference, and recovery guards matter chiefly by preventing harmful moves. This paper supersedes an earlier artifact release whose reported improvement arose from measurement defects that we identify. All source, raw traces, and generators are public. Index Termsheterogeneous embedded systems, asymmetric interconnect characterization, multiprocessing, Linux, RTOS, timing contracts, runtime adaptation I. INTRODUCTION Embedded platforms increasingly integrate two execution environments on one board: Linux application processor for libraries, networking, and developer productivity, and real-time microcontroller for isolation and predictable execution [1], [2]. task that can run in either domain faces placement choice whose consequences extend beyond compute time. Crossing the boundary adds serialization and transport, contention reshapes tail latency, and move may be illegal for stateful or Linux-specific operations. natural idea is to treat the microcontroller as refuge: when tasks timing degrades on Linux, move it to the real-time domain. Classical heterogeneous scheduling maps task graphs statically from cost estimates [3]; feedback scheduling adapts resources to measured error [4]; and runtime verification makes timing violations observable [5], [6]. What remains unclear on asymmetric LinuxRTOS boards is whether such move can actually help, and how runtime should decide when faster prediction is not sufficient permission to migrate. We study this question with QFabric, deliberately narrow prototype on the Arduino UNO Q. portable task declaration is compiled for both domains, profiled in each, and governed by an empirical contract. recovery controller applies hysteresis to complete observation windows, admits candidate only if semantic, capacity, and predicted-cost conditions hold, drains in-flight work at an epoch boundary, and commits the move only if post-switch probation confirms the contract; otherwise it rolls back. The central finding is boundary, not speedup. On this board every MCU invocation pays fixed dispatch cost of about 19 ms, and because that invocation is issued and relayed by Linux processes, Linux interference degrades the MCU path more than the Linux path. Migration therefore never improves contract in our measurements; QFabrics guards earn their place by refusing the moves that naive controller would make. An earlier artifact release [7] reported 36.6% improvement from recovery; Section VI-F identifies the measurement defects behind that result and shows that it does not hold. Contributions. This paper makes four contributions. First, it presents guarded recovery protocol that combines bounded wire ABI, effect-based semantic admission, quiescent epoch switching, and probation-based commit or rollback (Section IV). Second, it characterizes the UNO LinuxMCU interconnect across payload size, concurrency, load, and frequency governor (Section VII-A). Third, it reports matched-load measurement study of five workloads in both domains under three load conditions and two caller policies, decomposing each call into compute and residual dispatch cost (Section VII-B). Fourth, it evaluates the controllers decisions on four-node chain and shows through an ablation that hysteresis and probation prevent harmful migrations (Sections VII-CVII-D). Positioning. Approaches to cross-domain placement differ in when the assignment of software to execution resources is fixed, what triggers reassignment, and whether reassignment must prove its benefit before it is kept. Static mapping binds at design time [3]; asymmetric-multiprocessing frameworks and partitioning hypervisors bind at configuration time [2], [8], [9]; and feedback scheduling, mode-change protocols, and migration runtimes rebind at runtime but keep move once it is made [4], [10], [11], [12]. Section II describes the platform and system model, Section III reviews and compares related work, Section IV presents the design, Section the implementation, Section VI the methodology, Section VII the results, and Section VIII discusses implications and threats to validity before Section IX concludes. II. BACKGROUND AND SYSTEM MODEL C. Research questions We ask: RQ1, what does the LinuxMCU interconnect cost, and how does that cost respond to payload, concurrency, load, and frequency policy? RQ2, under matched load conditions, how do the two domains compare per call, and where does the time go? RQ3, on four-node chain, do contract violations arise, and does the controller decide correctly against deployable baselines and an oracle? RQ4, are hysteresis, admission, and probation necessary? RQ5, what does the mechanism itself cost? A. Target platform III. RELATED WORK The Arduino UNO combines quad-core Arm CortexA53 application processor running Debian Linux with an STM32U585 Cortex-M33 microcontroller running Zephyr [1]. Arduinos Bridge stack exposes MessagePack remote procedure calls in both directions through Linux-resident router process [13]. The arrangement resembles remote-processor systems built on remoteproc and rpmsg [14], [15], but we use the stock UNO stack rather than modifying the transport. Fig. 1 shows how QFabric sits on this platform: the policy, the dispatcher, and the Bridge router all execute in Linux userspace, so every MCU invocation begins and ends there. B. System model An application is chain = (V, E) of tasks. Each task may have Linux implementation, an MCU implementation, or both, together with fixed-width request and response types, numeric identifier, and an effect class. Only pure, bounded tasks are migration eligible. placement assigns domain d(v) {L, M} to every task. Every invocation is issued from Linux userspace, so the latency observed for task in domain decomposes into local compute and residual that captures dispatch, transport, and scheduling delay: Lv,d = Cv,d + Rv,d. (1) We review five lines of work that bear on cross-domain recovery and compare representative systems in Table I. Its first three columns follow the dimensions introduced in Section I: binding time, trigger, and the unit of isolation; the remaining columns record whether property is central to the cited work, not whether it could be added. A. Static and feedback-driven placement HEFT ranks task graph and maps it to heterogeneous processors using estimated computation and communication costs [3]. It is the natural static reference but does not monitor deployed timing. Real-time scheduling theory provides admission and schedulability foundations [19], and feedback scheduling adjusts resource allocation from runtime error [4]; autonomic computing generalizes the monitoranalyzeplan execute loop [20]. QFabric uses such loop, but its actuator is guarded change of execution domain. B. Timing contracts and runtime verification Runtime verification observes real-time behavior with bounded intrusion [5]. Stochastic contracts provide empirical runtime checks for component systems [6], while formal timing contracts and zone-based models support verification and synthesis [21], [22]. These works motivate our contract semantics; our focus is the operational protocol after violation. TABLE COMPARISON OF QFABRIC WITH RELATED WORK. Asymmetric multiprocessing and partitioning Heterogeneous SoCs that pair application cores with realtime cores are commonly run as asymmetric multiprocessing systems, with Linux managing remote RTOS through remoteproc and rpmsg; OpenAMP standardizes these interactions [2] and has been evaluated on real-time embedded SoC platforms [23]. Measurements on Zynq UltraScale+ show that inter-processor signaling can reach sub-microsecond latency when shared memory is used directly instead of the OpenAMP stack [24]. An alternative to physically separate cores is static partitioning hypervisor such as Jailhouse [8] or Bao [9]; their real-time behavior and interference on Arm platforms have been compared empirically [25], and hypervisor-based isolation has been combined with programmable-logic memory on heterogeneous MPSoCs [26]. In these approaches the assignment of software to cores or partitions is fixed at configuration time. QFabric takes the LinuxRTOS split and its transport as given, and changes only which side executes declared task after contract violation. D. Timing analysis and mixed criticality QFabrics contracts are empirical soft real-time bounds, not WCET guarantees. Static and measurement-based WCET analysis [27], and measurement-based probabilistic timing analysis in particular [28], [29], give principled ways to derive bounds from observed executions, under assumptions that our percentile thresholds do not establish. The mixedcriticality literature, started by Vestals model of tasks with several execution-time estimates of different assurance [16] and surveyed by Burns and Davis [30], also studies runtime adaptation when lower-assurance estimate is exceeded. That reaction is usually criticality mode change, wellstudied class of protocol [10]. QFabrics recovery can be read as narrow, cross-domain instance of this pattern: violated empirical bound triggers guarded, verified change of placement, not change of criticality mode, and we make no claim of certifiable guarantees. E. Migration across heterogeneous processors Real-time task migration has been studied for dynamic resource management in many-core systems with feasibility analysis [17], and Linux supplies deadline-aware scheduling mechanisms [31]. CoMOS provides processor-agnostic tasks and runtime migration across heterogeneous processors [11]; YASMIN supports functionally equivalent task implementations and user-space real-time mapping on heterogeneous COTS platforms [12]; and Awkernel brings DAG scheduling into an RTOS evaluated on physical hardware [18]. QFabric differs in its trigger (an observed empirical-contract violation), its guards (semantic eligibility and capacity admission), and its insistence on post-switch verification. To the best of our search, this combination on physical LinuxRTOS boundary is new; we claim no novelty for placement, profiling, feedback control, or timing contracts individually. Our measurements also bound when the combination can help, which prior work on migration typically does not report. IV. QFABRIC DESIGN Section II showed that every invocation, in either domain, begins in Linux userspace and that predicted improvement is only an estimate. QFabrics design therefore treats migration as hypothesis: it is attempted only when the evidence and the guards allow it, and kept only when observation confirms it. A. QTask declaration and bounded ABI QTask declaration is the single source for Linux and MCU artifacts. The generator accepts fixed-size scalars, records, and bounded arrays; it rejects pointers, dynamic arrays, recursive types, unsupported effects, and messages larger than the 988byte payload budget. Versioned big-endian headers carry magic value, message kind, task identifier, request identifier, payload length, and flags. Golden vectors are checked independently in Python, C++, and on the MCU, which turns serialization bounds and effect eligibility into auditable facts rather than conventions. B. Contracts and admission Profiles exclude warm-up invocations and retain raw observations; minimum sample count marks an estimator valid. (4) Empirical soft real-time MCU executor answers each request in single Bridge call that returns both the result and the compute time measured with the Zephyr cycle counter, so no diagnostic calls fall on the measured path. Requests carry 64-byte input block encoded in base64 (at most 96 characters), inside the 128-byte payload envelope that Section VII-A verifies; both executors share one decoder so that they perform identical work. Every result is checked against an independent Python reference. Instrumentation is layered. Reduced mode records core timing, full mode adds structured observations, and disabled mode measures the base call path. An optional kernel probe is evaluated separately and is not required for control. An LED-matrix status display has disabled, static, and 10/30/60Hz refresh profiles so that its cost is measured rather than assumed. All records carry schema versions, run identifiers, monotonic timestamps, outcomes, and mode metadata, and command-line audits cross-check source hashes, sample counts, derived deadlines, and reported numbers. VI. EVALUATION METHODOLOGY The evaluation asks whether the protocol of Section IV ever has beneficial move to make on real hardware, and what it does when it does not. This section describes how we measured both domains under matched conditions so that the answer is not an artifact of the measurement. A. Testbed and workloads Table II summarizes the setup. All measurements use one UNO with its stock Bridge stack. The five workloads span trivial task and compute sweep: signed 32-bit addition; bitwise CRC-32 over the 64-byte block; and 16-tap triangular Q15 FIR filter over 32 samples repeated 1, 64, or 512 times with pass-dependent perturbation, written FIR1, FIR64, and FIR512. B. Load conditions and callers Three conditions are applied for the whole duration of run. Idle applies no load. CPU load runs eight stress-ng CPU workers under SCHED_OTHER. sections.content: preempt. Under each condition both domains are profiled with an ordinary caller and with the caller and Linux executor at SCHED_FIFO priority 50, giving 12 profile runs and 120,000 retained invocations. C. Evidence classes We keep three evidence classes separate. Direct measurements are the per-call latencies above. Hardware scenarios exercise the real controller on the board and demonstrate one committed switch and one rollback. Ordered trace replay composes the measured traces into four-node chain: each task visit consumes the next sample of the relevant trace in measured order, which preserves autocorrelation and regime changes, and 500 chain observations are replayed per cell. Replay runs the protocol of Section IV exactly, including Eqs. (4)(8). It permits paired comparison across policies but is not equivalent to running complete application. D. Baselines Table III lists the policies. The oracle chooses, for every task visit, the faster of the two domains next measured samples; it is non-causal lower bound, not competitor. E. Statistics Primary metrics are p95 latency and deadline-miss rate. For per-call p95 we report 95% confidence intervals from circular block bootstrap (2,000 resamples, block length 50), which respects the short-range autocorrelation of measured traces. All tables, figures, and numbers in the text are generated from the raw traces by scripts in the artifact, which record input digests. F. Relation to the earlier release An earlier artifact release [7] included manuscript whose flagship result was 36.6% p95 reduction from recovery on replayed chain under Linux load. Re-examination found two defects. First, its Linux executor was new process per invocation, so Linux latency was dominated by process creation: 8.05 ms p95 for an addition, against 0.075 ms with the persistent executor used here. Second, the replay drew MCU latencies from idle traces while drawing Linux latencies from loaded traces, although every MCU call is dispatched through Linux and is affected by the same load. The present evaluation removes both defects and fixes its deadline rule and replay protocol in the repository before any new data was collected. Under the corrected method the earlier improvement does not hold. The earlier release remains available unchanged for transparency. VII. RESULTS We answer the research questions in the order of the argument: first what it costs to cross the boundary (RQ1), then whether migration can recover that cost per call (RQ2) or per chain (RQ3), and finally whether the guards matter (RQ4) and what they cost (RQ5). A. RQ1: Interconnect characterization All cross-domain costs in QFabric originate from the Bridge RPC path between Linux and the MCU, so we characterized it before deriving any contract. Each point is the mean of three repetition-level percentiles over 1,000 Linux-observed round trips, recomputed from 108,000 raw samples with zero failures. Under the default schedutil governor, an idle zero-byte echo has p50 of 7.74 ms and p95 of 8.85 ms, sustaining 127.2 sequential calls/s; at the largest demonstrated-safe payload, 128 bytes, p95 rises to 34.04 ms and the rate falls to 30.2 calls/s (Fig. 3a); latency grows nearly linearly with payload size. 256-byte probe caused sustained loss of MCU RPC service, so we make no claim beyond 128 bytes. Four stress-ng CPU workers lowered several medians but raised p95 by 5.5%23.5% across Linux-initiated calls. Pinning the performance governor did not remove this tail penalty (6.7%42.9%); it changed echo p95 by 11.1% to 1.3% at idle and by 0.2% to +10.6% under load. Frequency policy therefore does not explain the loaded tail. With concurrent 8-byte callers, aggregate throughput grows sublinearly from 96.75 to 257.31 calls/s (2.66) at one to eight workers, while p95 rises from 10.27 to 29.80 ms (Fig. 3b). Load increased throughput by 1.8%8.2% yet produced 115.82-ms outlier, so contracts must be derived from tails, not throughput or medians. B. RQ2: Matched-load per-call comparison Table IV and Fig. 4 compare the domains per call. At idle, an MCU addition takes 18.81 ms at p95 against 0.075 ms in Linux, 251 gap. Table decomposes the idle median with Eq. (1). The MCU residual stays near 19 ms for every workload, so dispatch, not compute, dominates the MCU path; and the MCU computes FIR512 34 more slowly than the Cortex-A53, so heavier kernels widen the gap rather than closing it. Load changes the picture in an instructive way. CPU load raises the ordinary Linux p95 to few milliseconds, which SCHED_FIFO caller removes almost entirely (Table VI, tuned Linux). Under RT contention, the Linux path keeps p95 below 2 ms with occasional stalls, while the MCU path degrades sharply, with p99 up to 400 ms against 17.0 ms for Linux. sections.content: RQ1 About 9 ms p95 per zero-byte call, rising with payload; tails grow under load regardless of governor. Linux is faster in every cell; MCU dispatch is fixed 19 ms and Linux contention hurts the MCU path more. RQ2 RQ3 No contract fails on Linux; QFabric correctly makes 0 switches in 30 cells. RQ4 Yes: without hysteresis, 7 harmful switches; probation rolls back 5. RQ5 decision costs about 177.2 µs, negligible against dispatch. rolls back 5 of these moves; the remaining two were still in probation when the trace ended (open at end). Hysteresis prevents the harmful moves, and probation bounds the damage when move is made anyway. E. RQ5: Mechanism overhead The mechanism itself is inexpensive. One policy decision costs 170.1 µs of CPU time and 177.2 µs of wall time at p95 over 1,000 in-process evaluations, with 3138-byte peak observed by tracemalloc; the latter excludes the interpreter baseline and is not total process memory. decision is thus two orders of magnitude cheaper than one MCU dispatch (18.81 ms at p95 for an idle addition). The worst LED-matrix refresh profile changes Bridge p95 by 2.05%. VIII. DISCUSSION A. When can cross-domain recovery pay off? Equation (1) makes the boundary explicit. Migrating task from Linux to the MCU helps only if Cv,M + Rv,M < Cv,L + Rv,L under the degraded condition. On this board Rv,M 19 ms at idle, Cv,M exceeds Cv,L by more than an order of magnitude, and the interference that inflates Rv,L inflates Rv,M at least as much, because both residuals are paid in Linux userspace. The inequality therefore fails for any task dispatched one call at time from Linux. Three architectural changes could reverse it: lower-latency transport such as shared-memory signaling, which reaches sub-microsecond latency on other heterogeneous SoCs [24]; dispatcher outside Linux userspace, for example kernel driver or partitioned core [25]; or MCUresident chains whose release is triggered by an MCU timer so that only inputs and results cross the boundary. Each is direct test of the boundary reported here. B. What the guards contribute Recovery and tuning solve different problems. When the workload can remain in Linux, SCHED_FIFO caller removes most CPU-load interference and is the right first step. The value of QFabrics guards is that they make adaptive placement safe to leave enabled: hysteresis ignores isolated stalls, admission rejects moves predicted to miss, and probation reverses moves whose benefit does not materialize. Table VII shows that plausible but unguarded controller would have turned submillisecond tails into 100-ms tails. C. Programmer effort task declaration states types, effect, and identifier once, and the generated ABI removes hand-written marshaling. The programmer must still supply semantically equivalent implementations for both domains, choose defensible contract, and state Linux-only effects; QFabric shifts effort from transport plumbing to contracts and equivalence rather than removing it. D. Threats to validity External validity. Results come from one UNO Q, one software stack, and five small kernels. Boards with faster transports or dispatch outside Linux userspace may reverse the inequality above. The chain results replay measured traces rather than running full application. Construct validity. Percentiles and miss rates do not establish worst-case execution time or hard real-time guarantees, and the admission test of Eq. (5) is utilization gate, not schedulability proof. The residual in Table is difference of medians, not measured component. Internal validity. All runs share one board and may be affected by firmware, thermal state, and background activity. Ordered replay preserves temporal structure within trace but cannot represent interactions between tasks executing concurrently. The deadline rule and replay protocol were committed to the repository before any Stage 12 data was collected. Baseline and load validity. SCHED_FIFO is strong but not exhaustive Linux baseline; SCHED_DEADLINE [31], CPU isolation, and affinity warrant comparison. The RT-contention co-runner is one synthetic pattern; synchronized or fully saturating interference would change magnitudes, though it would burden the MCU dispatch path as well. Safety scope. Quiescent switching prevents mixed-epoch calls in the prototype and effect annotations reject knownineligible tasks, but this is not proof of implementation equivalence. Production use would need state transfer, authentication, fault containment, and multi-client analysis. IX. CONCLUSION QFabric demonstrates guarded form of runtime adaptation across LinuxRTOS boundary: an empirical contract violation can trigger quiescent, admitted switch whose benefit must be observed before it is kept. Measured on an Arduino UNO with matched load conditions, the LinuxMCU path costs about 19 ms per call, the MCU computes up to 34 more slowly, and Linux interference reaches the MCU path through its Linuxresident dispatch. Migration consequently never improves contract in our study, the controller correctly declines to migrate, and an unguarded controller would have made harmful moves that only probation undoes. The broader lesson for heterogeneous embedded architectures is that the isolation offered by real-time core is available only to work whose dispatch also leaves the general-purpose domain. Testing faster transports, non-Linux dispatch, and MCU-resident chains is the natural next step.

sections.title: ARTIFACT AVAILABILITY
sections.content: The repository [32] contains source, generated code, unit tests, board sketches, raw and processed traces, campaign logs, audits, and the generators for every number, table, and figure in this paper; running make in the paper directory regenerates the assets and builds the PDF. The release cited here, v1.1.0, is archived on Zenodo with DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23692354.
